papers.abstract_en: In the classical art gallery problem, a guard sees a target when the segment joining them lies entirely within the polygon. We explore what changes when sight may bend along regular arcs on absolutely irreducible curves, but only those defined by primitive integer polynomials of total degree at most \(d\) and coefficient height at most \(H\). We call such curves admissible sight carriers.   Arcs can dramatically improve sight. In a one-sided comb, no straight-line guard sees selected targets in two different teeth, yet a single central guard sees a chosen target in every tooth along parabolic carriers.   Sight can also fail in two different ways. Geometrically, the polygon may block every sight arc of the allowed degree between two points. For instance, in an alternating comb, the number of guards needed for a row of targets spanning the comb grows linearly with the number of sides at each fixed degree, even for carriers with arbitrary real coefficients. Arithmetically, no admissible carrier may pass through the points at all. Even in the unit square, at fixed \(d\) and \(H\), the proportion of rational targets that must guard themselves tends to one as the height bound grows. An algebraic target may lie on no rational curve of degree at most \(d\), however large \(H\) is.   Both failures can be overcome for finite target sets by allowing the degree and coefficient height to grow. We show that every finite set of algebraic targets in a rational polygon becomes visible from any rational interior guard, with explicit bounds. We also construct, for every \(d\), arbitrarily large Galois orbits in the unit square, all of projective height \(4^{d+1}\), whose points must each guard themselves at degree \(d\) for every \(H\). Yet at degree \(d+1\) and coefficient height one, a single guard sees the whole orbit along \(Z(Y-X^{d+1})\).

papers.abstract_en: Softplus affine\((1,1)\) models keep the conditional mean positive while allowing coefficients of either sign. We study them under Poisson, negative binomial, gamma and related conditional distributions. A stationary solution with moments of all positive orders exists whenever the coefficient sum is less than one, strictly enlarging previously known sufficient regions. At the unit root, the coefficient sum equals one. Under an invertibility condition, a stationary solution exists in this case if and only if the intercept is negative. At a stationary unit root, the conditional mean has a power-law tail with an explicit index, and the observations can exhibit long memory. For a fixed softplus scale, the Poisson quasi-maximum likelihood estimator is consistent and asymptotically normal at the usual \(\sqrt n\) rate below and at the unit root, with the coefficient sum left unrestricted in estimation. At the unit root, these results require only a finite mean and yield standard Wald inference even when the observations have infinite variance or long memory. Simulations and two applications examine finite-sample inference and sensitivity to the softplus scale.

papers.abstract_en: Maintenance work orders are the largest written record of how industrial equipment fails, yet in most plants they are close to unusable for analysis. Short texts are abbreviated and misspelt, asset identity is buried in free text, work-type labels contradict the work described, and the fields that matter most for reliability (symptom, root cause, action taken) are usually empty. As a result, diagnostic knowledge stays with senior technicians and leaves when they do. We present Plant Memory, a system that applies technical language processing (TLP) to SAP Plant Maintenance (PM) exports and builds an ISO 14224-aligned maintenance ontology in which every extracted statement is a reified fact carrying a confidence score, the evidence it was read from, and a verification state. Extraction is rule-first, with an optional large language model (LLM) acting as a second reader whose disagreements raise a fact's review priority rather than overwrite it. Technicians verify facts through a review queue, answer targeted knowledge-gap questions where failures repeat without a recorded cause, and approve or reject ontology drift proposals when new terms appear. The resulting graph is served to people through a web application and to AI agents through a Model Context Protocol (MCP) server, so both query the same verified knowledge and every answer cites the work orders behind it. On a synthetic 12-month export of 400 work orders from a parboiled-rice plant, rule-based extraction reaches 96.2% component accuracy, 88.9% failure-mode accuracy and 100% root-cause precision at 62% coverage; on 28 diagnostic questions, ranked root causes from the ontology are correct at top-1 in 82.1% of cases against 53.6% for the raw SAP root-cause column.

papers.abstract_en: A finite Gödel chain generates not one integer sequence but a large family of them. The combinatorial mechanism is developed in a companion paper; here the sequences themselves are the primary objects. For $V_m=\{v_0<\cdots<v_{m-1}\}$, let $g_{j,n}^{(m)}$ count outputs equal to $v_j$, aggregated over all full bracketings on $n$ variables and all $m^n$ valuations. The root-pair refinement produces $N_{i,j}^{(m)}(n)=\sum_{r=1}^{n-1}g_{i,r}^{(m)}g_{j,n-r}^{(m)}$, with generating functions $N_{i,j}^{(m)}(x)=G_i^{(m)}(x)G_j^{(m)}(x)$.   We prove that the initial coefficients of these products uniquely identify the unordered root-value pair. Consequently, for each fixed $m$, there are exactly $\binom{m+1}{2}$ distinct root-pair generating functions. We catalogue the factories for $m=4,5,\ldots,10$, giving the first ten terms of every base sequence and every symmetric root-pair sequence. This range contains 49 base sequences and 210 symmetric pair classes, yielding 259 indexed sequence families before additional aggregates. The catalogue provides reproducible data for integer-sequence analysis and comparison with the On-Line Encyclopedia of Integer Sequences (OEIS).

papers.abstract_en: Reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards (RLVR) relies on costly model-generated responses, motivating larger rollout batches and square-root learning-rate scaling. Reported to approximately preserve progress per sample with one optimizer step per rollout, this rule is less understood in practical multi-step training. We develop a two-clock framework that separates the samples needed to make progress from those consumed before collapse. Under a local quadratic model, the square-root rule preserves first-order drift per sample but not progress: larger batches take fewer, longer updates and lose more to curvature, yielding a learning-rate-dependent critical batch beyond which sample efficiency degrades. A drift-threshold hypothesis predicts a complementary failure clock whose sample count remains approximately invariant along the square-root rule. Controlled GRPO experiments on Qwen2.5-Math-1.5B across a $16\times$ batch range support both predictions. Ratio clipping delays failure, especially for larger batches, but the progress gap persists without it. Widening the clip trades stability for a transient speed gain. The progress gap reappears on another dataset, a general-purpose checkpoint, and a 7B model. Finally, we use the two-clock framework to derive a simple multi-step RLVR schedule: start below the critical batch and switch to a larger batch before failure. Our code is available at: https://github.com/WinstonLiyt/two-clocks-rlvr.

papers.abstract_en: We study inference for continuous linear functionals of solutions to ill-posed inverse problems, including Euclidean parameters arising in nonparametric instrumental variables, proximal causal inference, and shadow-variable models. Although pointwise root-$n$ inference is possible under standard conditions, we show that this need not translate into locally reliable inference. Under a model imposing only minimal regularity conditions, the target is Hellinger discontinuous when both inverse problems are ill-posed: arbitrarily small changes in the data-generating law can produce arbitrarily large changes in the target, ruling out informative locally uniform inference. Imposing a uniform bound on a minimum-norm solution restores Hellinger continuity under regularity conditions, but does not by itself ensure stable root-n inference. If, in addition, both inverse problems are ill-posed and the solution whose norm is uniformly bounded is nonunique at a law $P_0$, then under regularity conditions the target fails to be pathwise differentiable; consequently, asymptotically linear estimators exhibit nonvanishing root-$n$ bias under some local alternatives, causing Wald confidence intervals to undercover asymptotically. Under regularity conditions, pathwise differentiability is restored if the uniformly bounded solution is unique at $P_0$. It is also restored, regardless of uniqueness, under the stronger requirement that the corresponding solution satisfy a uniformly bounded $β$-source condition for some $β$>0. We relate these regimes to very weak, weak, and strong identification in instrumental variables models.

papers.abstract_en: We argue that tacit knowing is better modelled as an operating regime of one memory substrate than as a kind of content. The substrate is VaCoAl, an algebro-deterministic XOR-and-shift hyperdimensional memory over GF(2), realized as CASRAM (commercial SRAM-CAM) and PyVaCoAl (DRAM-CAM).In VaCoAl/PyVaCoAl a directed acyclic graph (DAG) reads two ways. Repairing every collision (Rescue mode) makes the trace exactly auditable but ranks no path higher; tolerating collisions (Don't Care mode) yields a path-integrated confidence, CR$_2$, that silently favours direct routes. This audit-valuation complementarity is a formal counterpart of Polanyi's claim that tacit and explicit knowledge are not sharply divided. It separates contingent tacitness, which a new query brings out (AlphaGo's game tree), from regime-bound tacitness, statable only in a regime where it is gone (AlphaGo's hunches). (1) Polanyi's from-to structure reads as non-commutative binding, the Identikit as role-filler composition, recognition as majority-vote coincidence. (2) Explicating the valuation destroys it, as attending to his fingers can make Polanyi's pianist falter, yet a closed-form law states it. Polanyi, Nonaka, Tsoukas and Collins each capture part of this but narrowly; even Nonaka and von Krogh's continuum cannot tell contingent from regime-bound tacitness. (3) Collins's three tacit knowledges become strata, one outside the substrate. (4) Our mentor-student DAG is a tacit-transmission graph. (5) Terence Tao's remark that AI-solved problems spawn few follow-ups is diagnosed as rootless explicit knowledge: checkable results whose route no one can follow and that no one yet understands well enough to extend, teach or judge. To re-root them, LLMs generate, VaCoAl/PyVaCoAl keeps an auditable trace with its confidence, and people value, a role virtue epistemology shows cannot be offloaded. Testable predictions follow.

papers.abstract_en: An unknown ground excitation is recovered from the measured response of a rigid body sliding in two dimensions on an inclined surface under Coulomb friction, a system with no classical solution, whose sampled trajectories come from a time stepper. The Moreau stepper is shown to admit an exact inverse, explicit, non-iterative and vectorizable, giving the ground acceleration over each step in closed form, without regularization or an assumed source model. The inverse evaluates the friction direction at the end of the step, not its beginning. Inverting the continuous equation instead is not a secondary discretization choice: the two inverses differ by an exact identity proportional to the rotation of the sliding direction within the step, bounded by twice the frictional deceleration, which is of order one g for typical interfaces. The identity is inactive in one dimension, which explains why the sliding block literature has not confronted it. Verification against a manufactured reference solution recovers it to machine precision. On the field record, the discrepancy reaches 0.10g in root mean square, which exceeds the whole propagated uncertainty of the reported peak, and it suppresses 17% of the recovered travel, behaving as a bias, not noise, so root-mean-square agreement in acceleration understates it. The method is applied to surveillance video of a delineator post that slid in the 24 June 2026 La Guaira earthquake, yielding a peak ground acceleration of 0.912 +/- 0.047g, and a lower bound of 0.47g independent of the imagery. Displaced rigid bodies can therefore provide quantitative ground-motion information where instruments are absent.

papers.abstract_en: Although weak at normal gravity, gas radiation sets the gravity at which a co-flowing hydrogen jet diffusion flame stops flickering. Flamelet-based simulations with unity Lewis numbers, which reproduce the flicker frequency measured by femtosecond coherent anti-Stokes Raman scattering within 4%, are combined with local stability analysis. At one tenth of normal gravity, the adiabatic flame flickers, the radiating flame does not, and switching the emission off restores flicker. Radiation acts through two mechanisms that do not weaken at reduced gravity. The hot outer layer loses buoyancy in proportion to the gas residence time, and a disturbance that displaces the flame also displaces its emission, which damps the disturbance on the lean flank (displaced-emission damping). Freezing the radiative source, which removes only its response to disturbances, slows the downstream recession of the oscillation more than tenfold. Both mechanisms slow the upstream spreading of disturbances. This spreading, competing with the co-flow, sets the onset location and the critical co-flow. Without radiation, the spreading speed scales with the square root of gravity; its radiative reduction does not. At reduced gravity, the flicker limit therefore becomes a straight line relating the square root of the co-flow Froude number to a radiation number, the ratio of buoyant to radiative time scales. The calibrated line places the critical gravity for the experimental co-flow at 0.13 times normal gravity, 2.6 times the adiabatic value. It correctly predicted whether two further flames keep flickering. Beyond the limit, transient wave packets can mimic flicker throughout a short drop-tower test.

papers.abstract_en: Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) has emerged as a dominant paradigm for improving Large Language Model (LLM) by intertwining it with other components, such as a vector/graph database. Therefore, the resulting RAG systems are often highly configurable, under which a non-trivial amount of failures are related to the configurations. However, there remains a lack of systematic understanding regarding the configuration issues for RAG systems. To bridge this gap, in this paper, we conduct the first large-scale empirical study of 654 real-world configuration issues collected from 10 diverse RAG systems. Drawing on this, we provide a complete categorization of the symptoms, root causes, relevant stages, and fix patterns of configuration issues for RAG systems, as well as several new observations. Our findings not only reveal the characteristics of configuration issues, but also strongly link them to the unique pipeline stages of RAG, e.g., we found that most symptoms can be observed at the early or late stage, while the stage of the root cause might not be at the same stage as where the symptom is identified. We also provide nine actionable insights to the practitioners on testing, localizing, and fixing the configuration issues for RAG systems.

papers.abstract_en: Generalized Pellet's theorem is extended to analytic matrix-valued functions using Descartes' rule of signs for infinite series. Cauchy's estimate is incorporated to allow numerical computation of the bounds. To address the issue that Pellet's theorem and its generalizations may not always guarantee the existence of bounds, for the case of matrix size one, we employ the Dandelin- Lobachevsky-Graeffe method, which ensures the existence of the bounds for the roots and further improves them as the order of the transform increases. Without the need for any a priori information on the function, these theorems allow us to compute mathematically verified bounds for the roots in a certain region using an interval arithmetic implementation of the function. Numerical examples and an implementation are provided to illustrate the effectiveness of the proposed method.

papers.abstract_en: Long-horizon agentic RL is constrained by the futures visited by the current policy. When rollouts fail to reach useful behaviors, improved credit assignment cannot provide supervision for states and actions that were never encountered. On-policy distillation (OPD) introduces teacher guidance on policy-induced states, and recent multi-turn variants improve how this guidance is scheduled, replayed, refined, or validated. However, they do not directly use the oracle-controlled future itself as the training trajectory. We introduce \textbf{State-Rooted Executable Rollout Optimization (SERO)}, which augments on-policy agentic RL with executable oracle continuations. SERO restores a state actually reached by the current policy and lets a training-only oracle continue interacting with the real environment, making the downstream observations and oracle actions themselves available for learning. It then applies \textbf{policy-reachability weighting}, which weights each oracle step by the frozen behavior policy's compatibility with the preceding oracle actions. This allows deeper supervision to become effective as the policy becomes more compatible with the oracle branch. The oracle loss is optimized separately from the base RL estimator and no oracle is used at inference time. We evaluate SERO on two challenging interactive-agent benchmarks, ALFWorld and WebShop, using Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct and Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct. On ALFWorld, learning the full executable continuation is substantially more effective than supervising only the root oracle action, while policy-reachability weighting further improves out-of-distribution performance.

papers.abstract_en: Knowledge distillation (KD) improves language-model pretraining by matching teacher distributions at corpus prefixes, but provides no direct supervision at contexts induced by student predictions. We introduce PA1-OPD, which augments corpus-path distillation with teacher feedback after one student-sampled transition per selected prefix. This expands the supervised states while retaining next-token prediction and corpus-path KD. Data-anchored roots support parallel sampling, and differentiable tree attention shares prefix computation without changing inference. In two continued-pretraining settings, full coverage improves held-out cross-entropy over KD across C4, PG-19, and Pile at every evaluated checkpoint. In Stage2, selecting the 10% of roots with highest student surprisal adds 48.85% to KD's Macro cross-entropy gain over next-token training. Gains remain when branch supervision excludes successor states already on the corpus path, supporting the value of feedback beyond observed contexts. Additional depth or breadth improves aggregate results at unchanged per-term supervision weight, with benefits varying by corpus. These findings support local student-induced supervision as a complement to pretraining distillation.
